title: Amazon Bedrock Pricing (2026): Models and Token Costs
summary: Amazon Bedrock pricing uses a pay-per-use model with rates varying by AI model and pricing mode, letting you estimate costs before scaling automation…
body_markdown:
## Calling Bedrock models from Activepieces workflows


Activepieces has 742 integrations, counted from its MIT-licensed open source monorepo, and you can call a Bedrock model from a no-code flow through an HTTP request or MCP step, which is where you can control the bill.


Activepieces has its own pricing, separate from Bedrock's: Plus is $20 a month and Team is $200, so the two meters run side by side.


### Routing tasks to the cheapest adequate model


Bedrock meters by tokens, so the unit to manage is the call, and a flow lets you decide per call which model receives it.


A branch step can send short, repetitive work such as tagging a support email or extracting a date to a small, cheap model, and reserve the expensive model for drafting or reasoning.


You pay the premium rate only on the branch that needs it, which is how a cheap-looking rate stops being the deciding number.


A platform that resells you its own model has already made that routing decision and priced it before you open the product.


Activepieces doesn't resell one: the Bedrock model you pick is called on your own provider key, so the tokens from that HTTP request step land on your AWS account at your rate, and you can reach it from Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client.


The free plan is $0 with unlimited flows, and Bring-Your-Own-Key availability by tier is on the pricing page, so you can start for free with no flow constraints, but Bring-Your-Own-Key access depends on your tier. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


Three habits keep the meter honest:


1. Cap input length before the call, with a text step that trims a long email thread or document to what the task needs. Input tokens are billed whether or not the model uses them.
2. Set a maximum output length in the request body, so a verbose answer can't run up output tokens, which usually cost more than input.
3. Write each call's model, token counts and timestamp to a Google Sheets row. Without that log, you learn which branch is expensive only when the invoice arrives.


### Sending model output to the apps you already use


Once the model returns text, the flow passes it to the next step. The screenshot below shows the shape: a Calendly cancellation trigger feeds a Slack message step and a[Gmail](https://www.activepieces.com/pieces/gmail) email step, so one event fans out to two destinations.


Swap the trigger for a new support ticket and the HTTP request to Bedrock for the middle step, and the same layout posts a summary to a Slack channel, emails a draft reply through Gmail, or appends a row to a sheet.


That fan-out costs nothing extra on the Bedrock side, because the model is called once and its output is reused.


The cost to watch on the Activepieces side is credits: the free plan includes 1,000 a month, and when they run out flows wait for the next day's credits, so size long chains against that allowance.
